{{Short description|Open problem in convex geometry}}
{{technical|date=July 2026}}

[[File:Affine plank relative width example.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|The relative width of a plank is its width divided by the body's width measured in the same perpendicular direction. Here, the relative width is 2/6 = 1/3.]]

In [[mathematics]], the '''affine plank problem''' is an open question in [[convex geometry]] posed by [[Thøger Bang]] in 1951 as a strengthening of [[Tarski's plank problem]]. It asks whether the sum of the ''relative widths'' of any collection of [[plank (geometry)|planks]] covering a [[convex body]] must be at least&nbsp;1. Unlike the original plank problem, which was solved by Bang himself, the affine plank problem remains open in general, although it has been resolved for special cases including centrally symmetric bodies.<ref name="ball1991">{{cite journal |last=Ball |first=Keith |author-link=Keith Martin Ball |title=The plank problem for symmetric bodies |journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]] |volume=104 |issue=1 |pages=535–543 |year=1991 |doi=10.1007/BF01245089 |mr=1131482|arxiv=math/9201218 }}</ref>

The problem is also known as '''Bang's conjecture''',<ref name="verreault">{{cite journal |last=Verreault |first=William |title=Plank theorems and their applications: a survey |journal=[[Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society]] |year=2025 |doi=10.1112/blms.70230 |arxiv=2203.05540}}</ref> the '''affine plank conjecture''',<ref name="bakaev">{{cite arXiv |last1=Bakaev |first1=Egor |last2=Yehudayoff |first2=Amir |title=A note on the affine plank conjecture |year=2026 |eprint=2602.20290 |class=math.MG}}</ref> or the '''affine-invariant plank problem''';<ref name="chambers">{{cite journal |last1=Chambers |first1=Gregory R. |last2=Mouillé |first2=Lawrence |title=A note on the affine-invariant plank problem |journal=Rocky Mountain Journal of Mathematics |arxiv=1604.00456 |year=2022 |volume=52 |issue=1 |pages=117–126}}</ref> sometimes described as a geometric [[pigeonhole principle]].<ref name="ball1991" />

==Statement==

A '''plank''' in <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math> is the closed region between two parallel [[hyperplane]]s. Given a [[convex body]] <math>K \subset \mathbb{R}^d</math> (a compact convex set with nonempty interior) and a plank <math>P</math> with unit normal vector <math>u \in S^{d-1}</math>, the '''relative width''' of <math>P</math> with respect to <math>K</math> is

:<math>\operatorname{rw}_K(P) = \frac{w(P)}{w_K(u)},</math>

where <math>w(P)</math> is the width of the plank (the distance between its bounding hyperplanes) and <math>w_K(u)</math> is the width of <math>K</math> in the direction <math>u</math> (the distance between the two [[supporting hyperplane]]s of <math>K</math> perpendicular to <math>u</math>).

{{math theorem
| name = Conjecture
| note = Bang, 1951
| math_statement = If planks <math>P_1, \ldots, P_m</math> cover a convex body <math>K \subset \mathbb{R}^d</math>, then
:<math>\sum_{i=1}^m \operatorname{rw}_K(P_i) \geq 1.</math>
}}

Since <math>w_K(u) \geq w(K)</math> for every direction <math>u</math>, the relative width of any plank is at most its absolute width divided by the minimal width of <math>K</math>. Therefore, the affine plank conjecture implies [[Tarski's plank problem|Bang's theorem]] (the solution to Tarski's plank problem), making it a strictly stronger statement.<ref name="verreault" />

A key feature of relative width is its '''affine invariance''': if <math>T</math> is an invertible [[affine transformation]], then the relative width of <math>T(P)</math> with respect to <math>T(K)</math> equals the relative width of <math>P</math> with respect to <math>K</math>. This invariance is the reason for the name "affine plank problem".<ref name="ambrus2010">{{cite web |last=Ambrus |first=Gergely |title=Appendix: Plank problems |year=2010 |url=https://users.renyi.hu/~ambrus/appendix.pdf}}</ref>

==Equivalent formulation==

Alexander (1968) showed that the affine plank conjecture is equivalent to a geometric generalisation of the [[pigeonhole principle]]:<ref name="alexander">{{cite journal |last=Alexander |first=Ralph |title=A problem about lines and ovals |journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly]] |volume=75 |issue=5 |pages=482–487 |year=1968 |doi=10.2307/2314701 |jstor=2314701}}</ref>

{{math theorem
| name = Conjecture
| note = equivalent form
| math_statement = Given a convex body <math>K</math> in <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math> and <math>n</math> hyperplanes, there exists a translate of <math>\tfrac{1}{n+1}K</math> inside <math>K</math> whose interior does not meet any of the hyperplanes.
}}

Ball (1991) described this as a "multi-dimensional pigeon-hole principle".<ref name="ball1991" /> The equivalence connects the affine plank problem to [[Diophantine approximation]] via observations of [[Harold Davenport]] (1962).<ref name="alexander" /><ref name="kupavskii-pach">{{cite journal |last1=Kupavskii |first1=Andrey |last2=Pach |first2=János |author2-link=János Pach |title=From Tarski's plank problem to simultaneous approximation |journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly]] |volume=124 |issue=6 |pages=494–505 |year=2017 |doi=10.4169/amer.math.monthly.124.6.494|arxiv=1511.08111 }}</ref>

==Known results==

===Symmetric bodies===

The most important partial result is due to Ball (1991), who proved the conjecture for '''centrally symmetric''' convex bodies.<ref name="ball1991" /> Ball reformulated the problem in terms of [[Banach space]]s: every centrally symmetric convex body can serve as the unit ball of a finite-dimensional Banach space, and the conjecture becomes the statement that if the unit ball is covered by planks, the sum of their half-widths (relative to the norm) is at least&nbsp;1. Ball extended this result to infinite-dimensional Banach spaces in the same paper.

Ball's proof reduces the problem to a statement about matrices with 1s on the diagonal, then uses an orthogonal change of basis to symmetrize the matrix so that [[Tarski's plank problem#Bang's lemma|Bang's lemma]] can be applied. This approach also yielded a '''complex plank theorem''' for [[Hilbert space]]s.<ref name="ball2001">{{cite journal |last=Ball |first=Keith |title=The complex plank problem |journal=[[Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society]] |volume=33 |issue=4 |pages=433–442 |year=2001 |doi=10.1017/S002460930100813X}}</ref>

===Two planks===

Bang proved the conjecture for the case of two planks in 1953, with alternative proofs later given by Alexander (1968) and Gardner (1988).<ref name="alexander" /><ref name="gardner">{{cite journal |last=Gardner |first=R. J. |title=Relative width measures and the plank problem |journal=[[Pacific Journal of Mathematics]] |volume=135 |issue=2 |pages=299–312 |year=1988 |doi=10.2140/pjm.1988.135.299}}</ref><ref name="verreault" />

The conjecture remains open in the plane: Bang's 1953 result covers only coverings by two planks, not arbitrary coverings in&nbsp;<math>\mathbb{R}^2</math>.<ref name="bakaev" /> Even the case of three planks on a triangle is unsettled.<ref name="verreault" />

===Two directions===

Akopyan, Karasev, and Petrov (2019) proved the conjecture in the case where all planks have one of two normal directions, using techniques from [[symplectic geometry]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Akopyan |first1=Arseniy |last2=Karasev |first2=Roman |last3=Petrov |first3=Fedor |title=Bang's problem and symplectic invariants |journal=[[Journal of Symplectic Geometry]] |volume=17 |issue=6 |pages=1579–1611 |year=2019 |doi=10.4310/JSG.2019.v17.n6.a1|arxiv=1404.0871 }}</ref>

===Lower bounds===

For general convex bodies, the best known ''unconditional'' lower bounds on the sum of relative widths are:

* <math>\tfrac{1}{d}</math>, from combining [[John's theorem|John's ellipsoid theorem]] with Bang's theorem;<ref name="chambers" /><ref name="bakaev" />
* <math>\tfrac{2}{1+d}</math>, from combining Ball's symmetric-body result with a theorem of [[Hermann Minkowski|Minkowski]] and [[Johann Radon|Radon]];<ref name="chambers" /><ref name="bakaev" />
* <math>\tfrac{2}{1+\sqrt{d}}</math>, the current best bound, proved by Bakaev and Yehudayoff (2026).<ref name="bakaev" />

In the plane (<math>d = 2</math>), the Bakaev–Yehudayoff bound gives approximately 0.828. Their proof uses the [[support function]] and [[John's theorem|John's position]] of the difference body <math>L = \tfrac{1}{2}(K - K)</math>, combined with an inequality relating [[chord length]] to width for convex bodies inscribed between concentric balls.<ref name="bakaev" />

===Reduction to simplices===

Ambrus (2010) showed that the affine plank conjecture for <math>d</math> planks on all convex bodies in all dimensions reduces to verifying it for the regular <math>(2d-1)</math>-[[simplex]].<ref name="ambrus2010" /> The argument proceeds by choosing, for each plank direction, a pair of points in <math>K</math> that realise the width, then expressing the covering condition in terms of [[barycentric coordinates]] on a simplex formed by these points. This reduction means, for example, that proving the conjecture for three planks on the 5-dimensional simplex would imply it for three planks on any convex body in any dimension.

==Related problems==

* [[Tarski's plank problem]], the predecessor problem proved by Bang (absolute widths)
* The [[annulus plank problem]], asking whether removing a small homothetic copy from the interior changes the minimal total width needed for covering
* The [[Pyjama problem]], on covering the plane by rotated periodic stripes
* The '''Fejes Tóth zone conjecture''', proved by Jiang and Polyanskii in 2017,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jiang |first1=Zilin |last2=Polyanskii |first2=Alexandr |title=Proof of László Fejes Tóth's zone conjecture |journal=[[Geometric and Functional Analysis]] |volume=27 |issue=6 |pages=1367–1377 |year=2017 |doi=10.1007/s00039-017-0427-6|arxiv=1703.10550 }}</ref> which states that zones covering the unit sphere have total width at least <math>\pi</math>; its proof uses ideas from Bang's lemma
* '''Conway's fried potato problem''', solved by András Bezdek and Károly Bezdek (1995),<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bezdek |first1=András |last2=Bezdek |first2=Károly |title=A solution of Conway's fried potato problem |journal=[[Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society]] |volume=27 |issue=5 |pages=492–496 |year=1995 |doi=10.1112/blms/27.5.492}}</ref> which is related to the equivalent "pigeonhole" formulation

==Applications==

Through its connections to Bang's lemma and its equivalent formulations, the affine plank problem and its partial solutions have applications in several areas:

* '''[[Diophantine approximation]]''': The equivalent pigeonhole formulation yields results on simultaneous approximation of real numbers, sharpening estimates of [[Harold Davenport|Davenport]].<ref name="ball1991" /><ref name="kupavskii-pach" />
* '''[[Sphere packing]]s''': Ball used his plank theorem to give a lower bound for the density of [[lattice (group)|lattice]] packings of balls.<ref name="verreault" />
* '''Polynomial zero avoidance''': Glazyrin, Karasev, and Polyanskii (2023) developed a polynomial approach that unifies Tarski's plank problem with its complex and spherical variants, showing that a point on the unit ball at distance at least <math>1/n</math> from the zero set of any degree-<math>n</math> polynomial always exists.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Glazyrin |first1=Alexey |last2=Karasev |first2=Roman |last3=Polyanskii |first3=Alexandr |title=Covering by planks and avoiding zeros of polynomials |journal=[[International Mathematics Research Notices]] |volume=2023 |issue=13 |pages=11684–11700 |year=2023 |doi=10.1093/imrn/rnac259}}</ref>
